title: Keeping CRA Records
subtitle: Build an evidence trail that survives tax season

blocks.text: Good records tell the story of a sale or purchase without asking you to remember what happened eleven months ago. They link money in or out to an invoice, receipt, contract, log, bookkeeping entry and tax return. When those links agree, tax time becomes a quick review instead of a rebuild.

This is the last lesson in the Tax and Wealth course, and it ties the earlier lessons together through proof. Retirement choices need source documents. Estate files need current records. Self-employment and GST/HST numbers need sales and costs you can trace. Your record system is where every confident number earns the right to be confident.

This is general Canadian education, not personal tax or legal advice. Which records you keep, and for how long, depends on the tax, your business, the sale, any dispute and where you live. Check anything time-sensitive with the CRA, Revenu Québec where it applies, or a qualified professional. You’ll follow one sale through five links, aiming for a system another capable person could follow without opening a folder called “miscellaneous important things.”

items.title: “A bank statement is enough proof.”
items.text: A statement can show that money moved. It may not show what you bought, who sold it, why the business needed it or the GST/HST details you need to claim the tax back. The statement is one witness, not the whole cast.

blocks.text: Answer any CRA question in minutes, with proof already in hand.
blocks.detail: Records that link every amount to its source turn a review letter from a crisis into a short reply.
blocks.extra: Section 02 walks through the five links that make a record useful.

blocks.text: A record is more than a receipt. It can be an invoice, agreement, statement, photo, log, return, electronic file or anything else that shows what happened. The useful question isn’t “do I have paperwork?” It’s “can I trace this amount from the real sale or purchase to the return I filed?”

items.title: TRANSACTION
items.text: A sale, purchase, payment, refund, payroll run, equipment purchase or transfer happens.

items.title: SOURCE DOCUMENT
items.text: An invoice, receipt, contract, platform report, mileage log, deposit record or other proof captures it.

items.title: BOOKKEEPING ENTRY
items.text: The transaction is recorded with the right date, amount, account, tax treatment and business purpose.

items.title: RECONCILIATION
items.text: The entry is checked against bank, credit card, platform, payroll or government records.

items.title: RETURN OR REPORT
items.text: The checked totals flow into an income tax return, GST/HST return, payroll remittance, tax slip or financial statement.

blocks.text: If a link is missing, flag it for follow-up. Don’t invent it. A note explaining what happened and what proof is left is more useful than a beautifully sorted guess.

Give every transaction a reference number that never changes. Put the same number on the source document and the bookkeeping entry. Searching then becomes a straight path instead of a scavenger hunt designed by your past self.
Records have to explain the amount

Income records should show the date, amount and who paid. Expense records should usually show the date, seller, buyer, description and amount. GST/HST claims can also need the seller’s GST/HST number and your name, depending on the amount. The right record depends on the transaction: a signed contract may explain a deposit, a vehicle log explains kilometres and an email may confirm a price change. Keep whatever makes the number easy to understand.

sections.title: Capture Records Where the Transaction Happens

blocks.text: Waiting until year-end turns small gaps into expensive ones. Capture the record when the sale, purchase or payment happens.

For income, keep numbered sales invoices, cash register totals, online store and marketplace reports, payment processor statements, deposit records, contracts and credit notes. Record your full sales before platform fees or other deductions. Payment in cash, goods, services, foreign money or crypto can each need its own records and value.

For expenses, get a receipt and add the business reason when it isn’t obvious. A restaurant receipt shows food and tax but says nothing about who was there or why the meeting was for business. Add that while the meeting is still a memory, not a historical theory.

If a supplier doesn’t give you a receipt, the CRA says to write down their name and address, the amount, the date and what you bought in an expense journal, along with any other proof you have. That doesn’t guarantee you can deduct it, but it keeps the facts for review.
Use a three-step phone routine: photograph, label, file. Put the date, supplier, amount and purpose in the file name or record. “IMG_8472” is a camera’s opinion, not an accounting description.
Keep business and personal activity distinguishable

A separate business bank account and credit card cut down on mixed transactions. When a cost is partly personal, keep the full receipt plus the math behind the business share you claim. Don’t edit a receipt photo to show only the business part. Keep the original and attach your calculation, so the record shows the whole purchase and how you got your number. Refunds, rebates, chargebacks, store credits and cancelled orders need records too. Keeping the purchase while losing the refund leaves an expense that no longer matches reality, so keep both sides together.

sections.title: Close Each Month Before Opening the Next

blocks.text: Closing each month turns a pile of papers into records you can trust. Pick a fixed date and go through your accounts in the same order every time.

Start with each business bank and card account. Match the starting balance, each item, transfers, fees and the end balance. Then check payment processors and sales platforms, so total sales, platform fees, refunds and net deposits all connect.

Review money owed to you and money you owe. Confirm which invoices are unpaid and which bills are outstanding. Check that customer deposits, money you put in, money you took out, loans and transfers aren’t mistaken for sales or expenses.

If you’re registered for GST/HST, compare your taxable sales and tax charged with your GST/HST records, and review the receipts behind your ITC claims. If you have employees, check gross pay, deductions, employer contributions, net pay and remittances against your payroll records.

items.title: “Filing the return proves the records are complete.”
items.text: Filing online confirms that numbers were sent. It doesn’t prove every sale was captured, every expense was supported or every account was checked. A confirmation number is useful, but it isn’t a bookkeeping diploma.

blocks.text: Keep a short note for each month: accounts checked, missing items, corrections made, anything unusual and who reviewed it. Two minutes now can save an hour of explaining later.
Preserve corrections

Fix errors in a way that leaves a trail. Don’t delete a finished invoice or overwrite a checked entry without a record of the change. Use credit notes, adjusting entries and dated explanations. A correction should show the original amount, the new amount, the reason, the date and who made it. Your records don’t need to pretend nobody made a mistake. They need to show how it was fixed.
Noelle rescues the missing quarter
paragraphs: Noelle ran a small wedding-flower business in Fredericton. Customers paid her by invoice, e-transfer, card and through an online marketplace. She kept paper receipts in envelopes and trusted that her bank feed had caught everything else.

One fall, the CRA sent a letter asking her to back up her spring GST/HST return. Noelle opened her books and frowned. The marketplace deposits in her bank were lower than the sales on the marketplace’s own reports. Had she been underreporting sales?

Her first instinct was to add one big adjustment to make the numbers match and send it off. It would be quick. But she couldn’t have explained that number to anyone. Instead, she decided to follow each sale through the chain, one link at a time.

The marketplace report showed full sales, refunds, commissions and HST. Her bank showed only the money left over after all that. Her bookkeeping had recorded those smaller deposits as sales, so both her sales and her fees were too low. Two refunds were missing, and a few receipts didn’t have the supplier’s GST/HST number.

Noelle downloaded the original marketplace data, matched every payout to the bank and recorded sales and fees separately. She attached the refund reports and asked her suppliers for corrected invoices. Her bookkeeper reviewed the changes and wrote down what had been fixed and why. The CRA accepted her reply with one small adjustment.

Then Noelle made one more change. She added a monthly close day, and a quarter can’t be marked done until the marketplace totals match the bank. The envelopes are gone. In their place is a folder with a note on the front: “Sales are not deposits.”

blocks.text: Records you can trace turn a stressful letter into a simple reply.
blocks.detail: Following each amount back to its source lets you explain your numbers with confidence, and fix them cleanly when needed.
blocks.extra: Section 06 shows how to organize each type of record.

sections.title: Maintain Separate Tax and Business Files

blocks.text: One document can support more than one tax duty, but your filing system should show where each is used. Build a section for each of these groups.

items.title: INCOME TAX & FINANCIAL RECORDS
items.text: Keep proof of sales and costs. Keep your ledgers, bank and card statements, loans and contracts. Keep year-end notes, tax working papers, filed returns, notices of assessment, instalment proof and CRA letters. Property needs extra care. Keep the papers for buying, selling and fixing it up until long after you sell it.

items.title: GST/HST RECORDS
items.text: Keep sales and purchase bills and the tax charged. Keep proof of where each sale was made and why any sale had no tax. Keep credit notes, ITC math, working papers, filed returns, payment proof and CRA letters. Keep the working copy behind a return you filed online too.

items.title: PAYROLL RECORDS
items.text: Employee identity, hours, pay, taxable benefits, CPP or QPP, EI, tax withheld, employer contributions, remittances, TD1 forms, tax slips, returns and authorization letters. This information is sensitive. A shared folder called “everyone can edit” isn’t a control. It’s an invitation written in cheerful software.

items.title: VEHICLES & MIXED-USE ASSETS
items.text: Trip dates, destinations, reasons, business and total kilometres, running costs and odometer readings, plus purchase, lease, loan and sale papers. For home offices, phones, internet and other mixed-use items, keep the bill and the method you used to work out business use. Use it the same way each year, and write it down when it changes.

items.title: “My accountant or payroll company is responsible for keeping everything.”
items.text: Someone else can keep your records, but you or your business stay responsible for having them ready. Know what your provider holds, how to download it and what happens if the service ends.

sections.title: Keep Electronic Records Readable, Restorable and Secure

blocks.text: Filing online doesn’t end your duty to keep records. If your records are created or kept electronically, the CRA can ask for them in a readable, usable electronic form, even if you also have paper copies.

Download your data from bookkeeping, payroll, online store, payment, booking, mileage and crypto platforms on a regular basis. Keep reports that show every transaction, not just screenshots of dashboard totals. A screenshot shows what a screen looked like, but it may not give you the data to sort, trace or recheck the entries.

Test that you can restore your files. A backup is only a theory until a file can be recovered, opened and read. Pick one sample invoice, one bookkeeping export and one return working paper, and restore all three.

Keep backups in at least two protected places, with one away from your main device and business location. Encrypt sensitive records, use unique passwords and two-step login, limit access by role and remove access right away when a worker or provider leaves.

Keep a system map: each platform, what records it holds, how often you download them, where backups go, the file format, the account owner and how to recover it. Store login instructions securely, never in an ordinary worksheet.
Confirm where records are kept

The CRA generally requires records to be kept at your business or home in Canada, unless it gives written permission to keep them elsewhere. Records stored only outside Canada and viewed online from here don’t count as kept in Canada. Ask any cloud provider where your data is stored, how to download it and how long it stays available after you cancel. Get professional advice if your system depends on storage outside Canada, and keep a copy you control here.

sections.title: Retain the Right Records for the Right Period

blocks.text: The general CRA rule is to keep records and the papers behind them for six years from the end of the last tax year they relate to. That’s a starting point, not an automatic shred date.

Other timing can apply. If you file late, the six years count from the date you filed. Records linked to an objection or appeal must be kept until the dispute is settled and the appeal time has passed. The CRA can ask you to keep records longer, and records about property ownership and company history may need to be kept much longer or forever.
The duty to keep records can go on after a business closes. Companies, trusts, estates and charities each have their own rules. Some provincial laws may ask you to keep records even longer.

items.title: “Everything can be destroyed exactly six years after the purchase date.”
items.text: The usual rule counts from the end of the last tax year the record relates to, and several exceptions can make it longer. Shredders are efficient employees. They still need authorization.

blocks.text: Give each box or folder a “check before you shred” date, not a date to delete on its own. Before you shred, check a few things. Was the return late? Is there a dispute or a lawsuit? Does it touch property, payroll or GST/HST? Did the CRA ask you to keep it?
You need written CRA permission to destroy records before the six years are up. Ask using Form T137. Permission from the CRA doesn’t cancel duties under other laws.
Provincial and territorial variation

CRA rules are only one layer. Quebec businesses may need records for Revenu Québec tax, QST and payroll. Businesses in B.C., Saskatchewan and Manitoba may need records for their own sales tax. Payroll, job safety, work, company and privacy rules also change from place to place. Make a list of each province or territory where your business, staff, property, customers, registrations and licences are. An online business can pick up provincial duties without opening a provincial office.
Key takeaway

Strong records form a chain: capture the transaction, keep the source, record it accurately, check the account and link the checked total to the return. Keep electronic records readable and restorable, keep them for the right length of time and show your corrections instead of hiding them. The best record system isn’t the one with the most folders. It’s the one that can answer the next reasonable question.

After every return, create a yearly “proof package”: the final return, the filing confirmation, working papers, an income and expense summary, major elections, tax payments, the assessment, a list of source folders, software exports and any open follow-up items. The details stay in their usual folders. The proof package is just the map.

items.title: What are the five links in the evidence chain?
items.detail: The transaction, the source document, the bookkeeping entry, the check against outside records and the return or report you filed.

items.title: Why can a bank statement be insufficient support for an expense?
items.detail: It may show money moved without showing the item, the supplier, the business reason or the GST/HST details you need.

items.title: What should a monthly close note record?
items.detail: The accounts checked, missing items, corrections, anything unusual and who reviewed the month.

items.title: Why should data be exported from cloud accounting or platform services?
items.detail: You stay responsible for having records, and services, formats or providers can change. Downloads keep the full transaction detail.

items.title: Why isn't the general six-year retention rule an automatic destruction date?
items.detail: It counts from the end of the tax year, not the day you bought something. Late returns, disputes, property and other laws can make it longer.

sections.title: Your Action: Create Your One-Page Records-Control Map

blocks.text: Answer these six questions. This is fact-finding, not a filing.
Leave passwords, full account numbers, employee details, customer personal information and tax documents out of this form. This is a map of where your records live, not the records themselves.

items.title: Audit trail
items.text: A clear path from the first sale or purchase to each later entry, fix and total.

items.title: Backup
items.text: A separate copy of electronic files that can be restored after loss, damage or a system failure.

items.title: Books and records
items.text: Accounting information and the papers behind it, needed to work out and check your taxes.

items.title: Reconciliation
items.text: Comparing two sets of records, such as your ledger and your bank statement, to find and explain any differences.

items.title: Retention period
items.text: How long a record must be kept available.

items.title: Source document
items.text: The original proof of a transaction, such as an invoice, receipt, contract, statement or log.

items.title: T137
items.text: The CRA form to ask permission to destroy records before the six years are up.

items.title: Usable electronic format
items.text: A file format that can be opened, read and processed for review, not just viewed in a locked or outdated file.
